An anechoic chamber is a specialized test space that simulates a free sound field. Its interior is lined with structural sound absorbers that keep reflections extremely low, and such rooms are widely used for acoustic testing and research in consumer audio, aerospace, automotive engineering and other fields. Around the world, a handful of chambers stand out as true extremes: not only technically the best of their kind, but, thanks to their unique designs, milestones in engineering and acoustics. Join us on a tour of some of the most famous and unusual anechoic chambers in the world.

1. Microsoft Building 87 anechoic chamber, Redmond

  • Location: Redmond, Washington, USA

  • Completed: 2015

  • Performance: background noise as low as −20.6 dBA (certified by Guinness World Records as “the quietest room in the world”)

Microsoft’s Building 87 houses several acoustics labs, the most striking of which is its full anechoic chamber. Its walls, ceiling and floor are all covered with high-density fiberglass wedges, creating a space without reflections or echoes. To eliminate vibration transmitted through the building, the entire test space is isolated from the foundations by spring isolators, floating on a concrete floor below ground. As measured for Guinness World Records, the chamber’s background noise is as low as −20.6 dBA, close to the theoretical noise limit set by the Brownian motion of air molecules.

Applications: Microsoft uses the chamber to test how accurately Surface devices, Xbox audio systems, speech recognition microphones and other products reproduce and pick up sound. Because the room is so silent, staff generally cannot stay inside for long; some people hear their own heartbeat or the flow of their blood, and experience a kind of “sensory imbalance.”

2. NASA AAPL (Aero-Acoustic Propulsion Laboratory)

  • Location: NASA Glenn Research Center, Cleveland, Ohio, USA

  • Highlights: the world’s largest anechoic dome for aircraft engines, with a fully anechoic volume of more than 9,000 cubic meters

  • Completed: 1970s

The AAPL is a giant anechoic chamber built to study aircraft noise from jet engines and propulsion systems. It is built as an elliptical dome whose entire inner surface consists of more than 17,000 fiberglass wedges, creating a 360-degree echo-free environment that is especially suited to acoustic studies of high-thrust turbofan engines running on the ground. The structure also integrates a powerful airflow system that simulates intake and exhaust conditions in real flight.

Technical challenge: maintaining effective low-frequency absorption (20–200 Hz) in such a large volume is very difficult. It calls for specially designed oversize absorbing wedges, as well as independent foundations and vibration-isolated structures.

3. Orfield Laboratories anechoic chamber

  • Location: Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA

  • Performance: background noise as low as −9 dBA

  • Public program: open to the public for a “silence challenge”

This chamber once held the record for “the quietest room in the world,” until Microsoft broke it. Its interior is covered in extra-thick fiberglass wedges with exceptionally high absorption. What makes it special is that it serves not only to test industrial and medical hearing equipment but has also become part of art installations and public experiments. The “How long can you last in the dark?” experiment, for example, uses the room to probe the psychological limits of how much extreme quiet a person can bear.

Visitor feedback: when the noise drops to −9 dBA, the ear picks up all kinds of “self-noise” from inside the body, such as the heartbeat and faint creaks of the joints, and many visitors ask to leave within 10 minutes.

4. Apple Audio Lab

  • Location: Apple Park, Cupertino, California, USA

  • Size: about 1,000 square meters of audio engineering lab space in total

  • Highlights: a mix of room types, including full anechoic chambers, hemi-anechoic chambers and reverberation rooms

The audio lab at Apple Park has highly integrated acoustic test spaces, including several wedge-lined full anechoic chambers used to test microphone pickup, speech recognition and loudspeaker playback on AirPods, HomePod and MacBook. The lab is modular and goes beyond quiet-room testing to track parameters such as spatial audio and stereo diffusion. Apple engineers have also developed an in-house “virtual listening head” (artificial head) system, which models the user’s head and hearing and improves the spatial accuracy of the tests.

5. Chalmers anechoic chamber, Gothenburg, Sweden (Reverberation-Free Lab)

  • Highlights: a highly modular, panel-type anechoic chamber with removable absorbing panels

  • Focus: electric-vehicle motors and low-frequency interior noise

Unlike traditional wedge-lined rooms, this lab uses flat composite absorbing wall panels combined with adjustable low-frequency traps and polyhedral elements, to recreate a “free field inside the cabin” as closely as possible. Its test targets include evaluating the interior sound quality of new electric-vehicle drive systems in non-mechanical noise bands, such as high-frequency inverter noise and electromagnetic whine.

Summary: different designs for different missions

With the rapid growth of artificial intelligence, smart voice technology, low-noise aircraft propulsion and consumer audio, the demands on anechoic chambers are becoming both higher and broader. From ultra-quiet wedge-lined rooms to panel structures with tailored low-frequency absorption, a new generation of acoustics labs is becoming smarter, more modular and more application-specific. They are more than engineering spaces: they are a lever for technological innovation and the starting point for the future of hearing.
